title: Level 1: Hello World (LED Blinking)
aim: To write an Embedded C program that blinks an LED connected to Pin 13 (PB5) of the ATmega328P using direct GPIO register manipulation and a software delay loop.
objective: Understand how to configure GPIO direction using DDRx, drive a pin HIGH/LOW using PORTx, and produce a human-visible blink using a blocking software delay with _delay_ms().
theory:
The ATmega328P GPIO System

Every pin on the ATmega328P belongs to one of three 8-bit Ports: Port B (PB0–PB7), Port C (PC0–PC6), and Port D (PD0–PD7). Each port is controlled by a trio of hardware registers that you write to directly in memory.

DDRx — Data Direction Register

Before you can do anything with a pin, the CPU must know whether it is an input or an output. Writing a 1 to a bit in DDRx (Data Direction Register) configures that pin as an output. Writing 0 makes it an input (which also enables reading). For example: DDRB |= (1 << PB5); sets only bit 5 of Port B as an output, leaving all other bits untouched — this is the safest form using the bitwise OR-assignment operator.

PORTx — Output Data Register

Once a pin is configured as output, you control its voltage by writing to PORTx. Writing 1 drives the pin to +5 V (HIGH). Writing 0 drives it to 0 V (LOW). For inputs, writing 1 to PORTx enables the pin's built-in internal pull-up resistor (~20–50 kΩ), which is useful for buttons.

PINx — Pin Input Register

PINx is the read-only mirror of the actual voltage present on each pin. Reading it lets you check whether an external signal is HIGH or LOW. For outputs, PINx reflects whatever PORTx drives.

LED Circuit

An LED (Light Emitting Diode) passes current in only one direction and emits light when forward biased. Its forward voltage is ≈ 2 V for red LEDs. Since the MCU drives 5 V, a current-limiting resistor is mandatory to prevent damage. Using Ohm's law: R = (Vsupply − Vf) / If = (5 − 2) / 0.020 = 150 Ω minimum. A 330 Ω resistor is commonly used for safety margin, giving ≈ 9 mA of LED current.

Software Delay

The ATmega328P executes most instructions in a single clock cycle at 16 MHz, meaning it can toggle a pin millions of times per second — far too fast for the human eye (persistence of vision threshold ≈ 60 Hz). The _delay_ms() function from <util/delay.h> burns CPU cycles counting: at 16 MHz, 1 ms = 16,000 cycles. This is called a blocking delay — the CPU can do nothing else while waiting. It wastes energy and CPU time, which is why Experiment 5 replaces it with a hardware timer.

Key Registers at a Glance

  • DDRB (0x24) — Bit 5 = PB5 direction (1 = output)
  • PORTB (0x25) — Bit 5 = PB5 output level (1 = HIGH, 0 = LOW)
  • PINB (0x23) — Bit 5 = PB5 current voltage (read-only)

pretest.question: Which register is responsible for setting a pin as an Input or Output?
pretest.explanation: The Data Direction Register (DDRx) configures each pin's direction. 1 = output, 0 = input.

pretest.question: If you write '1' to a bit in the PORT register while the DDR bit is '1', what happens?
pretest.explanation: Writing 1 to PORTx when DDRx bit is 1 drives the output pin to +5 V (HIGH).

pretest.question: What is the forward voltage drop of a typical red LED?
pretest.explanation: Red LEDs typically have a forward voltage of about 2.0 V. This determines the resistor size needed.

pretest.question: Using a 330 Ω resistor with a 5 V supply and a red LED (Vf=2V), what is the LED current?
pretest.explanation: I = (5 − 2) / 330 ≈ 9 mA. This is within safe operating range for most LEDs.

pretest.question: What does the volatile keyword tell the C compiler?
options: May change unexpectedly, do not optimize reads
pretest.explanation: volatile prevents the compiler from caching a variable's value in a register, ensuring every read goes to hardware.

pretest.question: At 16 MHz, how many CPU cycles are burned by _delay_ms(1)?
pretest.explanation: 16 MHz means 16,000,000 cycles per second. 1 ms = 1/1000 s × 16,000,000 = 16,000 cycles.

pretest.question: Which header file provides basic I/O register definitions for AVR?
pretest.explanation: <avr/io.h> includes the MCU-specific header defining all peripheral registers like DDRB, PORTB, etc.

pretest.question: How many GPIO pins does the ATmega328P have in total?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P exposes 23 general-purpose I/O pins across Port B (PB0–PB7), Port C (PC0–PC6), and Port D (PD0–PD7).

pretest.question: Which bit operation safely sets only bit 5 of DDRB without touching other bits?
pretest.explanation: The bitwise OR-assignment (|=) sets the target bit to 1 while leaving all other bits unchanged.

pretest.question: What is the ATmega328P's maximum supported clock frequency?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P is rated for up to 20 MHz at 5 V. The Arduino UNO uses an external 16 MHz crystal.

procedure: Include the necessary headers at the top of your file: #include <avr/io.h> (for register definitions) and #include <util/delay.h> (for _delay_ms). Set #define F_CPU 16000000UL before including delay.h so the delay library knows the clock speed.
Define a constant for the LED pin to keep code readable: #define LED_PIN PB5. Pin 13 on the Arduino Uno physically maps to PB5 (Port B, Bit 5).
In setup() or before the main loop, configure PB5 as an output by setting its corresponding bit in DDRB HIGH: DDRB |= (1 << LED_PIN);. The (1 << PB5) expression creates the bitmask 0b00100000.
Start the infinite main loop: while(1) { ... }. The ATmega328P main loop must run forever — there is no operating system to return to.
Inside the loop, turn the LED ON by writing 1 to the PB5 bit of PORTB: PORTB |= (1 << LED_PIN);. This drives the pin to +5 V, forward-biasing the LED.
Call _delay_ms(1000); to hold the LED ON state for 1000 milliseconds (1 second). During this time the CPU is fully occupied counting empty cycles.
Turn the LED OFF by clearing bit PB5 in PORTB using AND-NOT: PORTB &= ~(1 << LED_PIN);. This drives the pin to 0 V, cutting LED current.
Call _delay_ms(1000); again to hold the OFF state for 1 second. The LED has now completed one full blink cycle (period = 2 seconds, frequency = 0.5 Hz).
Connect the hardware: LED Anode (long leg) → Pin 13 of Arduino → 330 Ω resistor → LED Cathode (short leg) → GND pin. Compile and flash the program, then observe the LED blinking at exactly 1 Hz.

posttest.question: Why do we need a resistor connected in series with the LED?
options: To limit current and prevent burning out the LED
posttest.explanation: LEDs have no internal resistance — without a current-limiting resistor, excessive current (limited only by trace resistance) would destroy the LED and potentially damage the GPIO pin.

posttest.question: What happens if you forget to set the DDR and leave it as input (0)?
options: Output writes to PORT are ignored — pin stays Hi-Z
posttest.explanation: If DDRx bit is 0 (input), writing to PORTx toggles the pull-up resistor, not the output voltage. The LED will not light.

posttest.question: What is the fundamental disadvantage of using _delay_ms() for timing?
options: It blocks the CPU — no other tasks can run
posttest.explanation: _delay_ms() is a busy-wait loop. The CPU cannot respond to button presses, sensor readings, or interrupts while waiting.

posttest.question: What is the difference between PORTB and PINB?
options: PORTB writes output; PINB reads actual pin voltages
posttest.explanation: PORTB drives output voltage (or enables pull-up on inputs). PINB reads the actual real-time voltage on the pin.

posttest.question: To toggle PB5 without affecting other pins in one instruction, what should you write?
posttest.explanation: The XOR-assignment (^=) flips only the specified bit. If it was 0 it becomes 1, and vice versa — perfect for toggling.

posttest.question: What tool converts C source to a .hex file for AVR?
posttest.explanation: avr-gcc cross-compiles C source to AVR machine code. avr-objcopy then converts the ELF to Intel HEX format for flashing.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: The ATmega328P has only Port B, C, and D. The 'A' naming is used on larger AVR devices like ATmega2560.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile memory. It requires continuous power to retain data. Variables in SRAM are lost on power-off or reset.

posttest.question: The blink period is defined as the time for one full ON-OFF cycle. With 1000ms ON and 1000ms OFF, what is the blink frequency?
In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: The AVR hardware clears the I (Global Interrupt Enable) flag in SREG upon entering an ISR, preventing nested interrupts unless explicitly re-enabled.

feedback: Excellent work! You've mastered the fundamental skill of embedded programming: direct register manipulation to control GPIO. Every complex firmware build on this exact foundation — DDR, PORT, PIN — the holy trinity of AVR I/O.
